t.1.40.1: O delight of the Raghus, King Sagara, knowing that his sons had been gone a long time, spoke to his grandson, who was blazing with his own splendour.
t.1.40.2: You are heroic and accomplished in learning, equal in splendor to your forebears. Seek out the fate of your fathers, and him by whom the horse was carried off.
t.1.40.3: There are creatures dwelling beneath the earth, mighty and huge. To ward them off, take up your bow along with your sword.
t.1.40.4: Saluting those who are worthy of salutation and slaying even those who cause obstacles, return successful in your purpose, bringing my sacrifice to completion.
t.1.40.5: Thus properly instructed by the great-souled Sagara, Aṃśumān, swift in his stride, took up his bow and sword and set out.
t.1.40.6: Urged on by that king, O best of men, he entered the subterranean path that had been dug by his great-souled fathers.
t.1.40.7: The one of great splendour beheld the elephant of the quarter being worshipped by Daityas, Dānavas and Rākṣasas, by Piśācas, birds and serpents.
t.1.40.8: Having circumambulated him and asked after his well-being, he then inquired about his fathers and about the one who had stolen the horse.
t.1.40.9: Having heard those words of Aṃśumat, the elephant of the quarter replied with affection: "Son of Asamañja, you will achieve your purpose and will soon return with the horse."
t.1.40.10: Having heard those words of his, he began to question all the elephants of the quarters, each in due order and in the proper manner.
t.1.40.11: Honored by all those guardians of the quarters, who understood speech and were skilled in words, he was urged on with the words, "You will return with the horse."
t.1.40.13: Then the son of Asamañja, overcome by sorrow, cried out in great anguish, deeply grieved at their slaying.
t.1.40.12: Hearing their words, he of swift stride went to the place where his fathers, the sons of Sagara, had been turned into heaps of ashes.
t.1.40.14: And there, not far off, that tiger among men, filled with sorrow and grief, saw the sacrificial horse wandering about.
t.1.40.15: Wishing to perform the water rites, that tiger among men looked about, but the greatly splendid one, seeking water, saw no pool or reservoir anywhere.
t.1.40.16: Then, casting a keen gaze all around, O Rāma, he saw the lord of birds, Suparṇa, the maternal uncle of his fathers, swift as the wind.
t.1.40.17: Then the mighty Vainateya spoke these words to him: "Do not grieve, O tiger among men; this slaying is approved by the world."
t.1.40.18: These mighty ones were burned by the immeasurable Kapila; therefore, O wise one, you ought not to offer them the ordinary water-libation of the world.
t.1.40.19: O bull among men, Gaṅgā, the eldest daughter of Himavant, the purifier of the worlds, would purify these who have been reduced to heaps of ashes.
t.1.40.20: These ashes, once moistened by that Gaṅgā, beloved of the worlds, will lead the sixty thousand sons to the world of heaven.
t.1.40.21: Go, O greatly fortunate one, and taking the horse with you, O bull among men, you should complete your grandfather's sacrifice, O hero.
t.1.40.22: Having heard the words of Suparṇa, that exceedingly valiant and greatly renowned Aṃśumān quickly took the horse and returned.
t.1.40.23: Then, O delight of the Raghus, approaching the king, who was consecrated for the sacrifice, he reported all that had happened, and likewise the words of Suparṇa.
t.1.40.24: Having heard that dreadful-seeming report of Aṃśumant, the king brought the sacrifice to completion according to the ordinance and in accordance with the prescribed rites.
t.1.40.25: The glorious lord of the earth, having completed his sacrifice, returned to his own city; but the king could reach no decision about bringing down the Gaṅgā.
t.1.40.26: Without reaching any resolution even after a long time, the great king, having ruled the kingdom for thirty thousand years, went to heaven.
